ledger.sentence: The NHS says screening is offered from age 50 up to the 71st birthday.
The first invitation comes between the ages of 50 and 53, and further invitations follow every three years until the 71st birthday.
Anyone registered with a GP as female is invited automatically.
People over 71 are not invited automatically but can ask for screening every three years.
For trans and non-binary people, invitations depend on the sex registered with the GP, and the NHS says people who have taken feminising hormones for more than two years can have screening.
A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast.
Each breast is pressed between two plates, which is likely to be uncomfortable, and some people find it painful, but it is over quickly.
Sources describe an appointment as taking roughly 20 to 30 minutes, and one unit suggests allowing up to an hour.
Results usually come within two weeks of the appointment and are also sent to the GP.
A normal result means another invitation in three years.
If the mammogram looks abnormal, the person is called back for more tests, such as a breast ultrasound scan or a biopsy.
The NHS says about four in every 100 women are asked to come back, and of these, one will be found to have cancer.
ledger.note: Summary: 4 in 100; one will have cancer.

ledger.sentence: Screening aims to find breast cancers at an early stage, when they are too small to see or feel.
It does not prevent breast cancer.
Mammograms use a very low dose of X-rays, and the benefits are judged to greatly outweigh that risk.
Screening does not always find a cancer that is there, so some people with breast cancer are missed.
A mammogram can flag something in a person who does not have cancer, which can cause anxiety and lead to more tests such as a biopsy.
Some people who are screened are diagnosed and treated for a breast cancer that would never have been found or caused them harm.
Screening is not a substitute for noticing changes, and a new lump, change in shape or nipple discharge needs a GP appointment, with no wait for the next invitation.

ledger.sentence: The NHS offers breast screening from age 50 up to the 71st birthday, with invitations every three years.
A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast, with each breast pressed between two plates.
Screening aims to find breast cancers at an early stage, when they are too small to see or feel, and it does not prevent breast cancer.
Screening can miss a cancer and can raise false alarms, and some people are diagnosed with a cancer that would never have caused harm.
NHS breast screening uses mammograms to look for cancers too small to see or feel. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment, results and harms.
